1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4.name: King's Gambit Accepted: King's Knight's Gambit

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 Bg7.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Traditional Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 Bg7.strategy: Declines the Muzio's wild complications: the bishop develops and backs the kingside chain, so Black can consolidate the extra pawn with a solid pawn structure. White keeps the centre and open lines, but has to prove that development and the f-file are worth a pawn without any knight sacrifice.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4.strategy: Drives the knight away at once and threatens both ...gxf3 and, once the knight leaves, a check on h4. It is the critical test of 4.Bc4: Black is a pawn up and White must pay for it with sacrifices. Sharp positions follow in which Black has to defend accurately but holds the material.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 d6.strategy: A quiet developing move: it frees the c8-bishop and takes the e5 square from White's knight, but it neither supports the g5-f4 chain nor strikes at the knight. White gets time to castle and build up against f7, so Black keeps the pawn without having solved how to meet the attack.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 Bg7 5.h.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Philidor Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 Bg7 5.h.strategy: Hits the g5 pawn, which is attacked twice and defended once, before the chain is complete. Black has to hold it at once, and White gains time to build a pawn centre. The result is a balanced game: Black's extra pawn is safe, but White has the lead in development and the choice of plan.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 Bg7 5.d.strategy: Takes the centre and opens the c1-bishop against f4, which only the g5 pawn holds. The d4 pawn is attacked by the bishop on g7 but defended twice. White plays for a big centre and quick castling; Black's chain holds, so it is a slower game than the Muzio, with White chasing development against a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 Bg7 5.O.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Hanstein Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 Bg7 5.O.strategy: Castles first and counts on the f-file and the lead in development, but does nothing against Black's plan to secure the pawn with a solid chain. Black consolidates at leisure, and the position is slightly more comfortable for Black.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 Bg7 5.d.strategy: Takes e5 away from White's pieces and stops the e4-e5 break, while freeing the c8-bishop. Black builds a compact centre behind the chain that holds the gambit pawn. White has to find play against a solid position, with the centre and development as the only compensation.

Supports the g5 pawn a second time, so the h-pawn lever loses its sting: after hxg5 hxg5 the bishop on g7 guards h8 and the rooks simply trade. The chain f4-g5-h6 keeps the extra pawn, and White has to find play with the centre.

Develops with a second attacker on d4, which is defended twice, so White must keep it supported or advance it. Black brings a piece out before the chain is finished, which leaves the g5 pawn resting on the queen alone.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 Bg7 5.d.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Mayet Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 Bg7 5.d.strategy: Adds a third defender to d4, which the bishop on g7 presses along the long diagonal, and frees the queen and the knight from guarding it. White keeps the broad e4-d4 centre as compensation, but the move is slow: Black's chain holds, so the attack has no fast target.

Castles at once, the usual course here: the king is safe before the position opens, the rook stands ready on the f-file, and the d4 pawn blocks the bishop on g7. White pays for the pawn with development and a broad centre.

Strikes at the head of the chain from the side. Black normally supports it with ...h6; if the pawns then trade on g5 the rooks come off on h8 and the bishop recaptures, so White wins nothing. The point is lasting pressure on the kingside, at the cost of a hole on g3.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 Bg7 5.h.strategy: Defends g5 a second time and builds the chain f4-g5-h6, with the bishop behind it. Without it the pawn on g5 would fall to the h-pawn and the knight. Black keeps the extra pawn for now, and White has to continue the fight for the centre.

Takes a second pawn and opens the g-file, but the knight recaptures at once. Black keeps the extra f-pawn and the strong bishop, but the kingside is open and White's pieces come out with tempo against it.

Pushes past the knight, but without ...h6 behind it the pawns are loose: 6.Ng5 lands with the bishop's help on f7, which only the king guards. Black ends up defending against an attack instead of enjoying the extra pawn.

Takes the centre and opens the c1-bishop on the diagonal towards f4 and g5, while the h-pawn keeps up the pressure on the chain. The d4 pawn is attacked by the bishop on g7 but defended twice. Black's extra pawn is safe only as long as the chain holds, so White plays for a lasting initiative.

Develops the queen's knight and supports e4 and d5 without committing the d-pawn. The bishop on g7 can trade itself for the knight, leaving White doubled c-pawns for the two bishops, so the move gives Black an easy way to relieve the pressure.

Supports e4 and opens the c1-bishop onto f4, a modest way to keep the gambit alive. It lacks the grip on the centre that a pawn on d4 gives, so Black gets time to finish development with the extra pawn.

Completes Black's set-up: the chain f4-g5-h6 holds the gambit pawn, the pawn on d6 takes e5 from the white pieces and the c8-bishop is free to develop. Black has a solid position with the extra pawn, and White must prove that the centre and the open lines are worth it.
Develops with a second attack on d4, which is defended twice, so White must keep it supported or push it. Black keeps ...d6 in hand and puts a piece on its best square, with the extra pawn intact.

Takes the pawn, but the knight recaptures and, with the d-pawn gone from d2, the c1-bishop now eyes the f4 pawn, which the g-pawn no longer shields. Black's extra material melts away, and the h6 pawn is weak.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 d6 5.O-.strategy: Castles at once, so a queen check on h4 no longer comes with tempo and the rook stands ready for the f-file. White accepts the pawn deficit for development and pressure on f7; Black has to show how to finish development and keep the extra pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 d6 5.h4.strategy: Hits the g5 pawn, which is attacked twice and defended once. Black cannot keep it: ...h6 loses a rook to hxg5 hxg5 Rxh8, and ...g4 drives the knight to g5, where it and the bishop both attack f7.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 d6 5.d4.strategy: Builds the centre and opens the c1-bishop onto f4, but ...g4 answers at once: Ng5 loses to ...Qxg5 and Nh4 to ...Qxh4+, so the knight has to go back. White keeps the centre for the pawn, but Black gains space and time.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 d6 5.O-.strategy: Develops the bishop with a threat to trade it for the knight, the piece that attacks g5 and blocks the f-file. The knight is defended three times, so White can recapture comfortably, but Black removes an attacker of the chain and keeps a simple position with the extra pawn.

Brings the bishop to its natural post, where it guards h8 against the h-file, eyes b2 and the centre, and meets the advance of the d-pawn at once. Black keeps the extra pawn behind the chain, and White has to prove the compensation.
Supports the g5 pawn a second time, so the h-pawn loses its lever, and builds the chain f4-g5-h6 with the f8-bishop still to come to g7. Black keeps the extra pawn and a solid position.

Puts the question to the bishop at once: it can trade itself for the knight, retreat or be supported. If Black trades, White recaptures with the queen or the rook and attacks f4 along the f-file; if the bishop retreats, White has gained space on the kingside.

Builds a pawn centre and opens the c1-bishop against f4, accepting the pin: if Black trades on f3, the queen recaptures with an attack on f4. White fights for the centre rather than for the pawn, while Black's g5-f4 chain remains its main asset.
A solid developing move that guards e4 and eyes d5, but it leaves the pinned knight and the g5-f4 chain alone. White is a pawn down for a slow initiative, and Black can trade on f3 whenever it likes.

Supports the bishop with a pawn instead of trading or retreating. If White takes on g4, ...hxg4 gives up a bishop for a pawn but opens the h-file against the king and attacks the knight. A bold, double-edged choice: Black plays for the attack at the cost of material.

Gives the bishop for the knight that attacks g5, so the g5-f4 chain loses its main enemy. White recaptures with the queen, which hits f4, and keeps both bishops; Black keeps the extra pawn but must watch the f-file and the c4-bishop's pressure on f7.

Keeps the bishop and the pin on the knight instead of trading, but the retreat can be challenged at once by the g-pawn, and Black's kingside is loosened further. Black holds the extra pawn for now, at the price of a bishop that White can harass.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Muzio Gambit, Wild Muzio Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.background: Giulio Cesare Polerio analysed it in the late 16th century, and the first recorded game, by Geronimo Cascio, appeared in Alessandro Salvio's Il Puttino of 1634. The English writer Jacob Sarratt gave it the name Muzio, misattributing it to Mutio d'Allesandro; it was most popular in the mid-19th century.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.strategy: The Muzio idea: White leaves the knight to be taken, castles to safety and wins a huge lead in development. Black has the material, White the initiative: the queen will hit f4, the rook backs the f-file and the bishop eyes f7. Black must defend accurately.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.d4.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Ghulam-Kassim Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.d4.background: Named after Ghulam Kassim of the Madras Chess Club, who analysed it in a short book published in 1829 and advocated it over the Muzio Gambit. Modern theory does not share that view, but his analysis was cited by Howard Staunton and the Handbuch des Schachspiels.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.d4.strategy: Also gives up the knight, but with the centre pawn: the c1-bishop attacks f4 and White builds a strong centre. It lacks the point of the Muzio, because the king stays in the middle and the rook does not join the f-file, so the attack comes slowly and Black can consolidate.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Nc.name: King's Gambit Accepted: McDonnell Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Nc.background: Named after the Irish master Alexander McDonnell, who successfully introduced it in his third match with Louis-Charles Mahé de La Bourdonnais. It has always been much less popular than the Muzio Gambit and is considered obsolete by Modern Chess Openings, but it has not been refuted.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Nc.strategy: Develops another piece rather than castling and offers the knight on f3, aiming for a lead in development and a kingside attack. It is regarded as inferior to the Muzio, since the king stays in the centre and the rook does not support the f-file, but it has not been refuted.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Salvio Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.background: It has almost disappeared from modern practice, since White's king is insecure after 5...Qh4+, and it is regarded as better for Black.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.strategy: Saves the knight with a second attacker on f7, but allows a queen check on h4 that forces the king to forfeit castling. White's king stays insecure, which is why the line is judged better for Black despite the pressure on f7.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.h4.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Australian Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.h4.strategy: Leaves the knight to be taken without the compensation of the Muzio. The h-pawn only keeps the queen off h4, while White's king is still on e1 and nothing yet supports the attack on f7. After ...gxf3 and Qxf3 Black is a clear piece ahead.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Bx.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Lolli Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Bx.background: Named after the Italian theorist Giambattista Lolli, whose Osservazioni teorico-pratiche of 1763 contains analysis of openings. It is considered obsolete, since Black can obtain an advantage by taking the bishop.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Bx.strategy: Gives up the bishop for a pawn to drag the king out, but the attack runs out of steam. After 5...Kxf7 6.Ne5+ the king can step back to e8, White wins back only a couple of pawns, and Black keeps the extra piece.
Takes the offered piece. The king steps onto f7, but nothing forces matters, so Black is a full piece ahead and can return the king to safety when the checks come.

Declines the bishop, but the pawn on f7 is lost for nothing and the king stays in the middle, unable to castle. White simply protects the bishop with the knight and keeps all the pressure, so Black has thrown away the free piece it was offered.

A second sacrifice: with the king already on f7, White castles and leaves the knight en prise again, hoping that open lines and the exposed king pay for two pieces. It is a desperate double gambit; Black has only to take and defend carefully.

Gives check and hits the g4 pawn, so White starts regaining material with tempo: the g4 and f4 pawns fall in the next moves. It is the most White can make of the position, but the bishop sacrificed on f7 is paid for with two pawns only.

Pulls the knight out of the g4 pawn's attack to the centre instead of sacrificing a second piece. White keeps its pieces, but without the check and the quick regaining of pawns it is simply a piece down for little, and Black can consolidate.

Takes the knight as well: Black is two pieces ahead, and the f4 pawn still shields the king on the f-file. White must show that open lines against the king are worth two pieces; Black's task is to untangle without walking into a mating attack.

Declines the second piece and puts the bishop on the long diagonal, where it eyes b2 and answers Ne5+ with ...Bxe5. Black stays a piece up, but gives White a move to rescue the knight and loses the cleanest way to cash in.

Develops the knight with an attack on e4 and keeps the capture on f3 in reserve. Black covers the king's flank, but the push e5 now comes with tempo against the knight, and the king stays on f7 where knight checks remain.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.d4.strategy: Takes the knight: Black is a piece up, and the pawn on f3 attacks g2 and cramps White's kingside. The centre pawn has opened the c1-bishop against f4, so Black must expect to give the gambit pawn back and rely on the extra piece.

Develops with an attack on d4 and keeps the capture on f3 in hand. The extra piece does not run away, but White gets a move to castle and keep the sacrifice alive, and Black gives up the cleanest way to cash in.

A calm developing move that opens the c8-bishop and guards e5, so the knight has no good square in the centre. The capture on f3 stays in reserve, but White gets a free move for the attack and Black does not take the piece when it is offered.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.d4.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Ghulam-Kassim Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.d4.strategy: Recaptures the pawn and attacks f4, which has no defender and is hit by both the queen and the c1-bishop. White regains a pawn at once and keeps a strong e4-d4 centre; Black is a knight up but has to deal with the threat to f4 and the bishop's pressure on f7.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.d4.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Kotov Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.d4.strategy: Takes the f4 pawn with the bishop and leaves the pawn on f3 for later, since g2 and the queen attack it. But that pawn attacks g2, so Black gets counterplay against White's kingside with tempo. It is a pawn grab that works only if White's development outweighs the knight.

Retakes with the g-pawn and opens the g-file, but ...Qh4+ follows at once and forces the king to move, so White loses castling immediately and has no cover left in front of the king. Black keeps the extra piece and the attack.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.strategy: The point of Black's play: the check wins a tempo and forces White to give up castling or block with g3. Black's queen is active, the g4 pawn is protected by it, and White's pressure on f7 has to wait. This is why the line favours Black.
Hits the knight with a developing move instead of checking first. White can simply take on g4 and regain the pawn, so the extra material is not secured, and the check on h4 loses much of its sting.

Kicks the knight and opens the c8-bishop to defend g4, but White takes on g4 anyway: after ...Bxg4 the queen recaptures, so the pawn is regained and the extra material is gone. Black gets a solid centre and easy development in return.

Steps out of the check and gives up castling, but keeps the knight on e5 and the pressure on f7. The king has lost castling for good, however: White gambles king safety for activity, which is why the line is judged better for Black.

Blocks the check with a pawn and keeps castling in hand, but ...fxg3 opens the f-file and the pawn on g3 attacks h2. White's kingside cover is torn apart and the knight is left on its own: a playable try that costs a second pawn.

Walks the king into the centre, where ...f3+ attacks it at once and opens the lines around it. White gives up castling for nothing and the king has no safe home, while Black keeps all its material and the attack.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Salvio Gambit, Silberschmidt Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.strategy: The safe choice: the knight guards both f7 and g4 and heads for f5, so White's pressure on f7 evaporates. Black keeps the extra pawn and simply develops while White's king is stuck on f1.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Salvio Gambit, Cochrane Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.background: Named after the Scottish master John Cochrane, whose Treatise on the Game of Chess of 1822 contained his own analysis of this variation of the Salvio Gambit.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.strategy: A counter-sacrifice: the pawn on f3 attacks g2 and opens lines against the king stuck on f1, and White can take it with the knight, the queen or the g-pawn. Black plays for the initiative rather than material, and the pressure on the king must be kept up.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Salvio Gambit, Viennese Variation
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.strategy: Another counter-sacrifice: the knight develops with an attack on e5 and leaves f7 attacked twice and defended only by the king, trusting in the exposed king on f1. Black plays for activity rather than material.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Salvio Gambit, Santa Maria Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.Ne.strategy: Defends g4 a second time and attacks the undefended e4 pawn, but leaves f7 attacked twice and defended only by the king. White has Nxf7 available, hitting the rook on h8, so Black must be sure of counter-chances against the exposed king. Playable, but it leaves the safest set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.strategy: Accepts the sacrifice and removes the attacker from f3: Black is a piece up. White then has to show that development and the pressure on f4 and f7 are worth the knight. This is the main test of the Muzio.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Muzio Gambit, Kling and Horwitz Counterattack
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.strategy: Another way to delay the capture: the queen covers f7 and attacks the e4 pawn, which has no defender. Black keeps the option of taking the knight later, but gives White time; the position is double-edged, and Black must be ready for sharp play against the king.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Muzio Gambit, Brentano Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.strategy: Counterattacks the bishop and the e4 pawn instead of taking the knight. But the delay lets White capture in the centre and open lines with tempo, and the attack that follows is strong. Black gains nothing by it.

Recaptures and takes up the Muzio post: the queen attacks the f4 pawn, and once it falls the queen and rook press down the f-file on f7 together with the bishop. White is a piece down but ahead in development, and Black must defend f4 and f7 accurately.

Retakes with the rook, which points at f4 but leaves the queen at home. The queen is not part of the f-file pressure, so the usual coordination of queen, rook and bishop against f7 is slower, and Black gets time to consolidate.
Retakes with the g-pawn and opens the g-file, but that also bares White's own king, and the pawn on f3 blocks the f-file along which the whole attack should run. Black's queen comes to h4 at once.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Muzio Gambit, Sarratt Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.strategy: Black's main defence: the queen defends f4, adds a defender to f7 and blocks the f-file, and from f6 it also eyes d4, so White cannot build a pawn centre with d4. Black stays a piece ahead and White must justify the sacrifice with another break.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Muzio Gambit Accepted, From's Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.strategy: Offers the f4 pawn as bait: if White grabs it, ...Qc5+ attacks the king and the bishop on c4 at once. The queen also covers f7, so Black can finish development in peace. A more reserved defence than the main one, but it sets a trap.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Muzio Gambit, Holloway Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-.strategy: Develops but ignores f4 and f7: after Qxf4 White regains the pawn and threatens Qxf7 mate, since the king has no flight square. Black is still a piece up and can defend with ...Nh6 or ...Qe7, but has handed White the initiative for nothing.
